study.title: Psalm 34 The deliverance of God, the fear of the Lord, and the way of wisdom
study.overview: Psalm 34 is a song of action of thanksgiving and instruction. David begins by inviting the humble to join in his praise, because he experienced that the Lord answers the cry, frees from the fears and surrounds those who fear him. Then the psalmist transforms his experience into teaching: true life encompasses correct words, separation from evil, the pursuit of peace and practical trust in God. In the end, the psalm contrasts the Lord's care for the righteous with the fate of the wicked, stating that the Lord is near the broken, frees from the afflictions and redeems the soul of his servants.

outline.title: Praise that calls the humble
outline.explanation: David decides to praise the Lord continually and invite others to magnify him with him. The focus is not only on your individual experience, but a shared worship that encourages the humble and afflicted to rejoice in the Lord.

outline.title: Witness of deliverance and invitation to prove the goodness of God
outline.explanation: The psalmist tells that he sought the Lord, was heard and delivered from fears and anguish. He teaches that the fear of the Lord includes obedient reverence and brings provision and assurance to those who seek him, even when others seem strong as lions.

outline.title: Practical Wisdom: how to live under the fear of the Lord
outline.explanation: David speaks as a teacher and teaches children and listeners to desire life and well. This involves controlling the language, abandoning evil, doing good and pursuing peace. The fear of the Lord is not mere feeling, but a concrete ethic.

outline.title: The Lord sees, hears, delivers and rescues
outline.explanation: The psalm ends with the contrast between God's attention to the righteous and their opposition to those who do evil. The righteous suffer many afflictions, but the Lord delivers them; he is near the broken, keep his life and redeems his servants from condemnation.

study.context: The title of the psalm links the song to an episode in which David changed his behavior before Abimelech and left. The notes explain that Abimelech is another name used for Achilles, and that the body of the psalm does not make an explicit connection with the narrated event. Thus, the episode serves as a backdrop, but the psalm surpasses the specific occasion and speaks in general about God's goodness to those who suffer.
study.theology: Theologically, psalm unites gratitude, wisdom and providence. God is not only remembered as a past deliverer, but recognized as a present: he responds, protects, hears, sees and rescues. The fear of the Lord appears as reverence that shapes conduct, not as a servile fear. There is also a strong theology of moral retribution: the righteous finds care and help while evil leads to ruin. At the same time, psalm does not promise the absence of suffering to the righteous; on the contrary, it states that afflictions are many, but never definitive. The Lord's closeness to the broken one reveals special care for the afflicted in spirit. The phrase about no broken bone can be understood, in the psalm itself, as an expression of the integral preservation of the life of the faithful; the notes also record that this text was applied to Jesus in the crucifixion, later Christian reading that does not nullify the original meaning, but extends it in biblical reception.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm is a song of wisdom that includes a hymn of thanksgiving, an invitation to wisdom and an exposition on the Lord's care for the needy and the fate of the wicked.
David, although he was a man of war and was already overwhelmed, did not consider underneath him to instruct the children and transmit spiritual counsel from his own experience.
The Lord redeems both the life and soul of his followers, continually preserving them from the danger and the definitive loss.

questions: In what situations have I spoken more of my fears than of the goodness of the Lord?
Does my search for God appear in a concrete way in my speech, my choices and in my search for peace?
How can I reflect today the care of the Lord for the broken and afflicted around me?
study.practice: This week, practice three attitudes of the psalm: praise God deliberately every day; watch his words, avoiding lies and malledice; and make a concrete gesture of peace, approaching someone afflicted with listening, prayer and practical help. Also, remember an occasion when God has delivered and transforms that memory into testimony, not into personal pride, but into encouragement to others.
study.uncertainty: The title of the psalm links the text to a historical narrative, but the notes observe that the body of the psalm does not explicitly make this connection. There is also a Christian reading, in the notes, that the verse on the unbroken bones was applied to Jesus, but this is a later reception, not necessarily the immediate sense of the psalm. Other than that, the available notes do not allow us to state more historical, geographical or linguistic details than those presented here.
